### Observed differences

- In the later window, A25 is followed by A32 or A33 in about 95 in 100 of its observed outgoing transitions (about 47–48 in 100 each), whereas before, A25 was followed by A26 in about 97 in 100; A26 now follows A25 in only about 1 in 100. [DIR001]
- The pairwise order between the two activity groups reversed: before, A26 preceded A32 in about 99 in 100 traces and A33 in about 99.5 in 100, and A28 preceded A32/A33 in about 99 in 100; in the later window, A32 precedes A26 in about 97 in 100, A33 precedes A26 in about 97–98 in 100, and A32/A33 precede A28 in about 96–97 in 100. [REL001, REL002, REL003, REL004]
- Downstream routing changed accordingly: before, A28 led to A32 (about 53 in 100) or A33 (about 45 in 100), and A32/A33 led mainly to A29 (about 46–54 in 100); in the later window, A28 leads directly to A29 in about 94 in 100 cases, while A32 and A33 lead mainly to A26 (about 47–49 in 100) or to each other, and almost never to A29 (about 1 in 100 or fewer). [DIR002, DIR003, DIR004]
- Step distances shifted consistently: A25→A26 went from mostly 1 step (about 97 in 100) to mostly 3 steps (about 92 in 100); A25→A32 and A25→A33 went from 4–5 steps to 1–2 steps; A28→A29 went from 3 steps (about 95 in 100) to 1 step (about 95 in 100); A32→A29 and A33→A29 went from 1–2 steps to 4–5 steps; A26→A29 went from 5 steps to mostly 3 steps. [LAG001, LAG002, LAG003, LAG004, LAG005, LAG007, LAG010, LAG011]
- Relative event positions moved the same way: A32 and A33 now appear earlier in the trace (mean relative position about 0.54–0.55 before, about 0.46 in the later window), while A26 and A28 appear later (about 0.43 to 0.51 and 0.49 to 0.57). [POS001, POS002, POS003, POS004]
- Three lag comparisons (A26–A33, A28–A32, A28–A33) rest on only 3–4 later-window observations and are excluded from the reading above. [LAG006, LAG008, LAG009]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the possibility that the block formed by A32 and A33 executes in a different place in the later window: it now runs directly after A25 and before A26, whereas before it ran after A28 and before A29 — in effect, the A32/A33 block and the A26–A28 segment swapped their sequence positions, and A29, which previously followed A32/A33, now follows A28 directly. [DIR001, DIR002, DIR003, DIR004, REL001, REL002, REL003, REL004, LAG001, LAG003, LAG004, LAG005, LAG007, LAG010, LAG011, POS001, POS002, POS003, POS004]

The support is direct and consistent: the four pairwise orderings reverse almost completely (about 97–99 in 100 one way before, about 96–98 in 100 the other way after); the successor changes at A25, A28, A32 and A33 point to the same rearrangement; the step-distance and position shifts match it; every item's difference exceeded 199 of 200 random re-split comparisons, 21 items were flagged against roughly 0.57 expected without change, and each item used rests on about 200 observations per window. [DIR001, DIR002, DIR003, DIR004, REL001, REL002, REL003, REL004, LAG001, LAG002, LAG003, LAG004, LAG005, LAG007, LAG010, LAG011, POS001, POS002, POS003, POS004]

An important competing explanation remains: the evidence shows the dominant executed order per window but cannot distinguish a re-routing within one variant from a shift in the mix of two pre-existing variants, since variant frequencies can differ between finite windows even without any structural change — although each window is near-deterministic (old order about 99 in 100 before, new order about 96–98 in 100 after), so such a frequency shift would have to be extreme. [REL001, REL002, REL003, REL004] Positions and lags are measured in event steps, so the change is established in sequence placement, not in clock time. [POS001, POS002, POS003, POS004, LAG001, LAG003, LAG004, LAG005, LAG007, LAG010, LAG011]
